  1. This entire phenomenon is mostly in my (and your) head.

The main reason we become silent is that we fear being ostracized by the crowd that once said that moral arguments weren’t good enough. This is not to say that ostracization isn’t possible, but we may find many others who are understanding or even supportive of a moral conversation.

1

Or ‘You do x and that’s bad, so who are you to talk?’ Or ‘Why do you care? This isn’t your business.’ Or ‘Must be nice to be able to think that way…’ etc. etc. These include all attacks that attempt to take away the initial party’s right to morality.

2

This is of course a much deeper historical event (and pattern) that can’t be done full justice with a few paragraphs about morals. This is ONE of the things that led to people turning a blind ‘moral eye’ to the enslavement of human beings.

3

Some people did make moral claims to argue for slavery in America, the most popular claim being the inferiority of the black race. As horrible as it sounds, that basis at least gives ground to a moral discussion, because it can be shown to be incorrect (and a poor argument for continued enslavement). Dismissing morality outright does not leave the open the door for conversation.

articles.title: Stepping Out
articles.subtitle: False futures and misidentifications
articles.description: False futures and misidentifications
articles.content:
Last week I wrote about my 7-day fast. As soon as I finished writing, I had an insight come to me: there is something very similar to my Vipassana experience in how I am anticipating the end of this.

The end seemed so exciting. I couldn’t wait to get that first bite of food, and then to continue on. But here’s the catch: there would come a time when I reached my limit and was satiated. Yes, food in the moment seemed super exciting, but then things would go back to normal. Food could not be a source of long-term, continual happiness.

During the 10-day Vipassana retreat, I felt something similar. I couldn’t wait to be done, to be able to experience regular things like reading books, exercising, and seeing people. I was craving stimulation so badly, and the same thing was true–once I got used to it, things would go back to normal.

It’s one of the sinister things that cravings do to us: they promise a better future, forever. They whisper in my ear that if I just get this thing, no problems will exist. It’s the only thing. And it’s never the case.

Vipassana Teaching

Luckily, during the meditation retreat, there were teachings on cravings. What they made me realize was that yes, I wanted to be done with the retreat, but there was no guarantee that anything would change afterward. If I gritted my way to the end because of the craving stimulation, I would go right back into the same cycles of craving and aversion that I lived in before.

​During my fast, I had a near-identical realization: I can simply look forward to eating for 7 days, but where does that leave me? Most likely, I will fall into a cycle of craving where my thoughts are generally centered around food. I realized then that I was caught between craving and fear.

​It’s a dark thought to have, one that says I don’t like where I am right now, but there’s nothing better to come afterward.

Luckily, I think there is something better (though I certainly had that thought in both instances).

Stepping out

One of the greatest aspects of Vipassana retreats is the coupling of experience with direction. Not only was I exposed to these high levels of craving and aversion, but I was also given an explanation as to what was really going on. Without that, the cycle just continues. Same with the fast. It could mean nothing if I just followed my impulses. I would eat a binge meal at the end of it, then go into a pattern of “living to eat”.

The solution, it seems, is to “step out” of the craving. That’s where learning can be done. That’s one of the huge benefits of challenging restrictive practices like these: it grants the opportunity to see the things that often run our lives.​

I recently read Louis CK’s new novel, Ingram, which was quite good. In it, Ingram, as a young boy, describes a “hunger dog” in his stomach that he would notice whenever he hadn’t eaten for a long enough time. When it got bad, Ingram feels as though he becomes the hunger dog, rather than the hunger dog simply being a part of his current experience.

We have all likely had the experience of being so entangled with a singular element of our existence that it becomes everything: pain is an easy one to relate to. When I am in great pain, I lose a sense of my identity. Everything in my experience is simply pain. When I’m working out really hard, that becomes everything. There is no me, just the task and all the associated pain. That’s being identified.

Stepping Out is doing the opposite, recognizing the element of existence that had taken over the identity for exactly what it is. There were many moments when I was very bored at the Vipassana center, and every ounce of me wanted to be rid of the experience. That became who I was. I was “desire”, I was “craving”. Fasting, there were moments when I just wanted to be done. That was me. That was it. Then I stepped out.

I realized that I could see the craving or the hunger for what they were, which are false promises. This is not to say they are bad–not eating is not a sustainable way to live. But they are still telling lies. My hunger impulse doesn’t tell me, “Eat something healthy, you’ll feel great after, and we’ll have lots of energy.” It says, “Let’s eat the best tasting thing, I promise you’ll be happy. You won’t have to worry about anything else. Trust me.” When I saw that story, there was no more identification. I was no longer the “hunger dog”.

Where to go

The important question remains: what happens after I step out? If cravings are promising me false futures, then how do I actually create happiness?

I think the answer lies outside of desire. Following desire, in my experience, tends not to lead to fulfillment. The things that I have found to lead me there came through trial and error, through living life and seeing how the actions I take impact my internal experience.

However, it is only after noticing impulses and cravings that I can even begin to decide to do those things. Otherwise, I am bound to remain in the same cycle of chasing false promises.
